Test case for {@link MullerSolver Muller} solver.

Muller's method converges almost quadratically near roots, but it can be very slow in regions far away from zeros. Test runs show that for reasonably good initial values, for a default absolute accuracy of 1E-6, it generally takes 5 to 10 iterations for the solver to converge.

Tests for the exponential function illustrate the situations where Muller solver performs poorly.
Test of solver for the sine function.
Test of solver for the quintic function.

Test of solver for the exponential function.

It takes 10 to 15 iterations for the last two tests to converge. In fact, if not for the bisection alternative, the solver would exceed the default maximal iteration of 100.

Test case for {@link MullerSolver Muller} solver.

Muller's method converges almost quadratically near roots, but it can be very slow in regions far away from zeros. Test runs show that for reasonably good initial values, for a default absolute accuracy of 1E-6, it generally takes 5 to 10 iterations for the solver to converge.

Tests for the exponential function illustrate the situations where Muller solver performs poorly.
Maximum number of iterations allowed for the solver in all tests.

Computes the acceptable tolerance for a root-finding result.

The tolerance is the larger of the solver's absolute accuracy and the product of the expected value's magnitude with the relative accuracy, matching the convention used throughout the solver's own stopping criteria. @param solver the configured solver whose accuracy settings are queried @param expected the analytically known root value @return the maximum allowed deviation between {@code expected} and the computed result

Test of solver for the sine function.

Verifies two roots of sin(x): x = π in [3, 4] and x = 0 in [-1, 1.5].

Test of solver for the quintic function.

The quintic function has three roots: x = 0, x = 1, and x = -0.5. Each is found in a bracketing interval that isolates exactly one root.

Test of solver for the expm1 function (e^x - 1).

The only root is at x = 0. Three increasingly wide bracketing intervals are tested to show that the solver relies on bisection fallback for wide intervals (convergence may take 10–15 iterations instead of the typical 5–10).
Medium interval: bisection fallback kicks in
Wide interval: bisection fallback is essential to stay within MAX_EVAL

Test of invalid parameters for the solver.

Two invalid inputs are tested:

  • A reversed interval [1, -1] where min > max, which must throw {@link NumberIsTooLargeException}.
  • A valid interval [2, 3] that does not bracket any root of sin(x), which must throw {@link NoBracketingException}.
expected: min > max is not a valid bracketing interval
expected: sin(x) has no root in [2, 3]
